en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Jewels 88.
The Training Rule on Silk Cloth.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks had couches and benches made upholstered with cotton down.
People, while wandering on a tour of the monasteries, saw this and complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, have couches and benches made upholstered with cotton down, just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures?"
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... they grumbled, complained, and criticized, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks have beds and benches made upholstered with cotton?"... [and so forth]...
“Is it true, monks, that you have had beds and chairs upholstered with cotton down?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
"How indeed, you foolish men, can you have a couch or a chair made upholstered with cotton down?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Whatever monk should have a bed or a chair made upholstered with cotton down, there is an offense of expiation involving tearing it apart.
Whoever, however, means whoever of such a kind... [and so forth].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Bed" (mañca) means:
There are four kinds of beds: one with legs shaped like elephant trunks, one with legs bound with bundles of cloth, one with legs shaped like crab claws, and one with detachable legs.
A chair is said to be of four kinds:
one with legs shaped like elephant trunks, one with legs bound with bundles of cloth, one with legs shaped like crab claws, and one with detachable legs.
"Cotton" means three kinds of cotton: tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, and pod-cotton.
"Should have [it] made" means...
Whether she does it herself or causes it to be done, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the effort.
Upon obtaining [the material], having torn it out, a confession of an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) must be made.
If she completes what was begun by herself, there is an offense of expiation.
If one completes what was begun by oneself through others, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one completes what was begun by others through oneself, there is an offense of expiation.
If one completes what was begun by others through others, there is an offense of expiation.
If one makes it or causes it to be made for another purpose, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one uses what has been obtained as having been made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense—
The waist-band, the body-binder,
and the shoulder-strap.
He makes a foot-cloth, a water-strainer, or a bolster.
If one obtains what was made by another, peels it off, and consumes it—
except in the case of one who is insane or is a first-time offender.
The sixth training rule concerning stuffing with cotton is finished.
